opus-5.5.text:
If you look back at the history of robotics over the past several decades, the field as a whole was really centered on one main battlefield: industrial manufacturing. Most of the robots that were actually deployed at scale were robotic arms on factory lines, in automotive plants, electronics assembly, welding, painting, palletizing, and so on. So the research and engineering focus naturally followed where the money and the deployments were.

What characterizes that setting is that the environment is highly structured. The parts arrive in the same position every time, the lighting is controlled, the fixtures are precise, and the task is repeated millions of times. In that world, what matters most is precision, speed, repeatability, and reliability. You don't need the robot to understand anything. You program a trajectory, maybe with very careful calibration, and it executes that trajectory again and again. So traditional robotics put enormous effort into things like kinematics, dynamics, control theory, motion planning, and high-precision hardware: very good reducers, servo motors, and so on.

And I think that was the right focus for its time, because that's where robots could create value. But it also means the field developed a certain mindset: the robot is essentially a programmable machine, and intelligence is mostly the engineer's intelligence encoded in advance. The robot itself doesn't generalize. If you change the product on the line, you have to re-engineer, re-program, sometimes redesign the whole cell.

The gap that's become very clear is that the vast majority of the world, our homes, stores, hospitals, warehouses with huge numbers of SKUs, even many parts of a factory, is unstructured. Objects vary, positions vary, people move around, tasks change. Traditional robotics never really solved that, because its methods were built on the assumption of structure. That's why for a long time you saw robots doing amazing things on a car assembly line, but almost nothing in everyday life.

So for me, the shift we're seeing now, toward embodied intelligence, is precisely about moving the focus from "how do we execute a predefined motion perfectly" to "how does a robot perceive, understand, and act in a world it hasn't seen before." That requires generalization, and generalization requires learning, data, and models in a way the traditional paradigm simply wasn't designed for. That, I think, is the fundamental transition the field is going through.

r001.rationale: It links factory deployments in structured settings, where precision and repeatability mattered, to the field’s focus on control theory and high-precision hardware.

r002.rationale: It mentions repeatability and control theory, but does not identify stable control algorithms as necessary for industrial robots’ repeatability.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. The way I see it, traditional robotics was built around a very specific kind of environment: the factory. If you look at where robots were actually deployed over the past several decades, it was overwhelmingly in industrial settings, such as automotive assembly lines, electronics manufacturing, welding, painting, and palletizing. And that deployment reality shaped the entire research agenda.

In a factory, the world is structured. You know exactly where the part will be, within millimeters. The lighting is controlled. The task repeats thousands of times a day without variation. So the central problems became precision, repeatability, speed, and safety in a fenced-off cell. Enormous intellectual effort went into kinematics, dynamics, control theory, trajectory optimization, and making a six-axis arm reach the same point a million times with sub-millimeter error. That was the right focus for that world, and it produced real economic value.

But there was a cost. Because the environment was engineered to remove uncertainty, the robot never had to deal with it. Perception was often reduced to a fixture or a simple sensor. The robot did not need to understand what an object was, only where its pre-programmed grasp point was. Generalization was not a goal, because the task never changed. So in a sense, traditional robotics solved the problem by making the world simple rather than by making the robot intelligent.

I think that explains the gap we feel today. The places where robots did not get deployed, such as homes, hospitals, restaurants, and ordinary warehouses with mixed goods, are precisely the places where the world cannot be engineered away. Objects are novel, cluttered, deformable, and the task is slightly different every time. The classical toolkit is still essential for executing motion, but it says very little about how to perceive and decide in an open world. That is why the field is now turning toward learning, large-scale data, and generalizable manipulation. We are not discarding the old focus. We are finally confronting the part of the problem that the factory let us postpone.

r001.rationale: The response ties traditional robotics’ focus on control theory and six-axis arms to factory demands for precision, repeatability, speed, and safety.

r002.rationale: It identifies repeatability as a central industrial robotics problem and connects it to extensive work on control theory and repeatedly reaching the same point accurately.

astra-6.text:
I think traditional robotics was shaped very strongly by where robots were deployed, primarily in factories. Those environments are structured and controlled: parts arrive at known positions, tasks are clearly defined, and people are often separated from the machines. So the focus was on precision, repeatability, speed, and reliability—doing the same operation consistently, over and over.

That also meant you could engineer the environment to make the robot’s job easier. The robot didn’t necessarily need to understand a changing world. When you move into homes or other everyday settings, that assumption breaks down. Objects move, people behave unpredictably, and tasks vary. So perception, learning, and adaptation become much more central.

r001.rationale: The response links factory deployment conditions to priorities such as precision and repeatability, but does not connect those priorities to hardware design and control.

r002.rationale: It identifies repeatability as an industrial robotics priority, but does not say stable control algorithms are necessary to achieve it.

sol-6.1.text: I think the historical focus of traditional robotics was closely tied to where robots were deployed, mainly in factories. Those environments were structured and controlled: the objects, the workspace, and the task could all be defined in advance. So the emphasis was on precision, repeatability, and efficiency—doing a particular motion reliably, over and over. That approach made a lot of sense for industrial deployment. But when you move robots into homes or other everyday environments, those assumptions start to break down. The robot has to deal with variation and uncertainty, which puts much more emphasis on perception, adaptation, and generalization.

r001.rationale: The response links factory deployment to precision, repeatability, and efficiency, but does not identify hardware design and control as the historical emphasis.

r002.rationale: It mentions repeatability and reliable motion, but does not state that stable control algorithms were necessary for industrial robots to achieve it.
